blocks.text: Masterpiece Games: "SimCity" and the Art of Gardening
Most video games have a clear goal: defeat the monster, rescue the princess, or get the highest score.
But in 1989, a game appeared that broke all these rules.
That game was SimCity, created by Will Wright.
SimCity had no "Game Over" and no "You Win."
It was a game about building and managing a city.
Players zoned land for residential, commercial, and industrial use, built power plants, and laid down roads.
But the true genius of SimCity lay in what the player could not control.
The Accidental Discovery
Will Wright was only 24 years old when he began developing the prototype for SimCity.
Interestingly, the idea came by accident.
While creating his first game, a helicopter shooter called "Raid on Bungeling Bay," he built a tool to design the game's maps.
He soon realized that designing the islands and cities with this "Map Editor" was far more fun than flying the helicopter and destroying them.
Combined with his background in architecture and the influence of Montessori education—which values self-directed learning—he decided to turn this map editor into a game itself.
He wanted to create a "software toy" where players could explore and create, rather than just win or lose.
Steven Johnson and "Emergence"
To understand the magic of SimCity, we must first look at a concept popularized by science writer Steven Johnson.
In his famous book "Emergence," Johnson asks a simple question: How do ants create such complex colonies without a leader?
Ant queens do not give orders.
Instead, each ant follows simple local rules.
When thousands of ants do this, a high-level intelligence "emerges" from the bottom up.
This phenomenon is not just found in nature.
It is also the secret behind SimCity.
The Architect vs. The Gardener
In traditional games, the player is like a god or an Architect.
You decide exactly where everything goes and exactly what happens.
However, Will Wright designed SimCity differently.
He adopted this Bottom-up approach, reflecting the biological systems described by Johnson.
Wright often compared the role of the player not to an architect, but to a Gardener.
A gardener can prepare the soil and plant the seeds, but they cannot force a flower to bloom.
They can only create the right environment for growth.
Similarly, in SimCity, you cannot force people to move into your city.
You can only lower taxes, reduce crime, and build parks.
If the environment is good, the "Sims" (citizens) will move in on their own.
The Traffic Jam You Didn't Program
A perfect example of this is the traffic jam.
Will Wright did not write a specific line of code that said, "Create a traffic jam at 5 PM."
Instead, he programmed simple rules for individual citizens: "They hate long commutes" and "They want to go to the nearest workplace."
When thousands of citizens followed these simple rules simultaneously, traffic jams emerged naturally on the screen.
This is exactly what Steven Johnson calls "Emergence."
It is a complex order arising from simple local rules.
Why It Matters Today
Before SimCity, we thought of systems as things we needed to control perfectly from the top down.
But SimCity taught us that trying to control everything often leads to failure.
Sometimes, the best way to build something great—whether it's a city, a software project, or a team—is to stop trying to be the Architect.
Instead, we should become Gardeners.
We should set the rules, nurture the environment, and wait for the unexpected genius to emerge.
